newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Former minister to run Brazil re-election panel.
newsitem.headline: Former minister to run Brazil re-election panel.

text.p: Odacir Klein, Brazil's former transport minister who resigned in disgrace in August after being involved in a hit-and-run accident, will preside over a lower house committee to discuss re-election, an official said.

The five other committee nominations from the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB) will only be made next Tuesday, the day before the government hopes to kick off its re-election battle in Congress, a PMDB spokeswoman said.

Klein resigned after a car driven by his son, and in which he was travelling, struck and killed a pedestrian but failed to stop. The former minister said his son had not obeyed his orders to stop the vehicle.

A constitutional amendment, allowing President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, state governors and mayors the chance of second terms, has to be approved by the lower house committee before advancing to the floor of the lower house.
The chances of the first meeting of the committee actually taking place on October 29 now depend mainly on the Brazilian Progressive Party (PPB).
The PPB is formally consulting its members on whether it should ignore a resolution passed earlier this year which banned the party from discussing re-election until 1997.
A PPB spokesman said the consultations would take until Saturday and no nominations would be made until October 29 at the earliest.
"From where we stand, the chances of the committee being set up (on October 29) aren't good," the spokesman said.
The PPB is reportedly reluctant to join the re-election debate before a second round of municipal elections on November 15 when the party is expected to win the Sao Paulo mayoral race.
Furthermore, the PPB is dominated by outgoing Sao Paulo mayor Paulo Maluf whose presidential ambitions may turn the party against re-election.

The government hopes to begin committee-level deliberations as soon as possible because it wants the re-election amendment through the lower house by February, when its pro-reform president Luiz Eduardo Magalhaes stands down.
